cards.title: A dual basis
cards.front:
In ℝ², use the basis b₁ = (1, 1) and b₂ = (1, −1). A dual basis consists of two linear functions φ₁ and φ₂: φᵢ(bⱼ) is 1 when i = j and 0 otherwise.

Find explicit formulas for φ₁(x, y) and φ₂(x, y). Verify the four required values. Write each function as ax + by.

Allow about 4 minutes to answer and 1 minute for feedback. Stop at 60 minutes total. Read the feedback once, then move on.
cards.back:
Write φ₁(x, y) = ax + by. Its required values give a + b = 1 and a − b = 0, so φ₁(x, y) = (x + y)/2.

For φ₂, the equations are a + b = 0 and a − b = 1, so φ₂(x, y) = (x − y)/2.

Thus φ₁(b₁) = 1, φ₁(b₂) = 0, φ₂(b₁) = 0 and φ₂(b₂) = 1. These functions extract the coefficients of a vector in the chosen basis; they are not the basis vectors themselves.

cards.title: Stable rank and ordinary rank
cards.front:
For a nonzero matrix A with singular values σ₁ ≥ σ₂ ≥ ⋯ ≥ 0, its stable rank is (σ₁² + σ₂² + ⋯)/σ₁². Its ordinary rank is the number of nonzero singular values.

Construct a diagonal matrix with ordinary rank 100 but stable rank less than 2. Specify all its diagonal entries and calculate both ranks. Explain in one sentence why there is no contradiction.

Allow about 4 minutes to answer and 1 minute for feedback. Stop at 60 minutes total. Read the feedback once, then move on.
cards.back:
One example is A = diag(1, 0.01, …, 0.01), with 99 copies of 0.01.

All 100 diagonal entries are nonzero, so rank(A) = 100. Its stable rank is 1 + 99(0.01)² = 1.009 < 2.

Ordinary rank counts every nonzero direction; stable rank measures the total squared stretching relative to the strongest direction. Many weak directions can contribute very little to stable rank.

cards.title: A quadratic conjugate
cards.front:
Let f(x) = 2x² for real x. Its Fenchel conjugate is defined by f*(y) = sup over real x of [yx − f(x)], where y is fixed.

Find f*(y) as a formula in y. Show which x attains the supremum and why it is a maximum. Keep the maximizing input and the maximum value distinct in your answer.

Allow about 5 minutes to answer and 1 minute for feedback. Stop at 60 minutes total. Read the feedback once, then move on.
cards.back:
Complete the square:

yx − 2x² = −2(x − y/4)² + y²/8.

The squared term is nonnegative, so the expression is at most y²/8, with equality exactly at x = y/4.

Therefore f*(y) = y²/8. The maximizing input is y/4; the conjugate is the attained value y²/8.

cards.title: The largest possible tail probability
cards.front:
A random variable X is nonnegative and has mean E[X] = 3. No other information about its distribution is given.

Find the largest possible value of P(X ≥ 12). Prove that no larger value is possible, and give a distribution of X that achieves your answer.

Allow about 3 minutes to answer and 1 minute for feedback. Stop at 60 minutes total. Read the feedback once, then move on.
cards.back:
Whenever X ≥ 12, its contribution to the mean is at least 12. Since X is nonnegative elsewhere, 3 = E[X] ≥ 12P(X ≥ 12). Thus P(X ≥ 12) ≤ 1/4.

This bound is attained by P(X = 12) = 1/4 and P(X = 0) = 3/4. The mean is 12/4 = 3, so the largest possible probability is exactly 1/4.

cards.title: The scale of a sample mean
cards.front:
X₁, …, Xₙ are independent and identically distributed, with mean µ and variance σ², where 0 < σ² < ∞. Write X̄ₙ = (X₁ + ⋯ + Xₙ)/n.

Find the factor cₙ > 0 for which cₙ(X̄ₙ − µ) has variance 1. Derive it from the variance of the sum, then state the limiting distribution given by the central limit theorem. Do not assume the Xᵢ themselves are normal.

Allow about 4 minutes to answer and 1 minute for feedback. Stop at 60 minutes total. Read the feedback once, then move on.
cards.back:
Independence gives Var(X₁ + ⋯ + Xₙ) = nσ², so Var(X̄ₙ) = σ²/n.

Therefore Var[cₙ(X̄ₙ − µ)] = cₙ²σ²/n. Setting this equal to 1 gives cₙ = √n/σ.

The central limit theorem says √n(X̄ₙ − µ)/σ converges in distribution to N(0, 1). For finite n the variance is exactly 1, but the distribution need not be exactly normal.

cards.title: Compressing a signal in time
cards.front:
For an integrable function f on ℝ, define its Fourier transform by F(s) = ∫ℝ f(t)e−2πist dt. Here s is frequency and i² = −1. Let g(t) = f(3t), and let G be the Fourier transform of g using the same convention.

Express G(s) in terms of F. Derive the formula by changing the integration variable. Your answer should show both the factor outside F and its new argument.

Allow about 4 minutes to answer and 1 minute for feedback. Stop at 60 minutes total. Read the feedback once, then move on.
cards.back:
Start with G(s) = ∫ℝ f(3t)e−2πist dt. Set u = 3t, so t = u/3 and dt = du/3.

Then G(s) = (1/3)∫ℝ f(u)e−2πi(s/3)u du = (1/3)F(s/3).

Compressing time by a factor of 3 spreads the frequency scale by a factor of 3 and multiplies the transform amplitude by 1/3.

cards.title: Can principal logarithms be added?
cards.front:
For nonzero complex z, define Log z = ln|z| + i Arg z, with Arg z in (−π, π]. Let z = w = e3πi/4.

Does Log(zw) = Log z + Log w hold for these values? Calculate both sides and explain any difference using their arguments.

Allow about 3 minutes to answer and 1 minute for feedback. Stop at 60 minutes total. Read the feedback once, then move on.
cards.back:
Log z + Log w = 3πi/4 + 3πi/4 = 3πi/2.

But zw = e3πi/2 = −i, whose principal argument is −π/2. Thus Log(zw) = −πi/2.

The right side exceeds the left side by 2πi. Adding the two principal arguments leaves the allowed interval, so the argument of the product must wrap back into it.

cards.title: How much can a fixed point move?
cards.front:
Maps T and S take a metric space into itself. The distance between two points is written d. Suppose T has fixed point p, S has fixed point q, and, for every x and y:

d(Tx, Ty) ≤ ½d(x, y), and d(Tx, Sx) ≤ 0.1.

Prove that d(p, q) ≤ 0.2. Give the short chain of inequalities. Existence of the two fixed points is already assumed; you do not need to prove it.

Allow about 4 minutes to answer and 1 minute for feedback. Stop at 60 minutes total. Read the feedback once, then move on.
cards.back:
Use p = Tp and q = Sq, and insert Tq:

d(p, q) = d(Tp, Sq) ≤ d(Tp, Tq) + d(Tq, Sq) ≤ ½d(p, q) + 0.1.

Subtract ½d(p, q) from both sides. This gives ½d(p, q) ≤ 0.1, hence d(p, q) ≤ 0.2.

The contraction prevents a small change in the map from causing an arbitrarily large change in its fixed point.

cards.title: Checking the regularity condition
cards.front:
For n = 2ᵏ with integer k ≥ 1, consider T(n) = 2T(n/2) + f(n), where f(2ᵏ) = 4ᵏ[2 − (−1)ᵏ]. Define f(1) by the same formula with k = 0.

The usual third case of the Master theorem requires a constant c < 1 such that 2f(n/2) ≤ cf(n) for every sufficiently large n.

Does this f satisfy that regularity condition? Calculate 2f(n/2)/f(n) separately for even and odd k, then give your conclusion. You do not need to solve the recurrence.

Allow about 5 minutes to answer and 1 minute for feedback. Stop at 60 minutes total. Read the feedback once, then move on.
cards.back:
The ratio is ½[2 + (−1)ᵏ]/[2 − (−1)ᵏ].

When k is even, it is 3/2. When k is odd, it is 1/6. There are arbitrarily large even k, so no fixed c < 1 can bound every sufficiently late ratio.

The regularity condition fails. It is not enough that n² ≤ f(n) ≤ 3n²: the condition also controls how the work changes between adjacent recursion levels. Failure of this condition prevents this direct use of the theorem; it does not by itself determine T(n).

cards.title: Combining two sigma-algebras
cards.front:
Let Ω = {1, 2, 3}. Two sigma-algebras on Ω are:

𝒜 = {∅, Ω, {1}, {2, 3}}
ℬ = {∅, Ω, {2}, {1, 3}}.

Is the collection 𝒜 ∪ ℬ itself a sigma-algebra? Answer yes or no and justify it using a closure requirement. The union here combines the two collections; it does not automatically add unions of their member sets.

Allow about 4 minutes to answer and 1 minute for feedback. Stop at 60 minutes total. Read the feedback once, then move on.
cards.back:
No. The collection contains {1} and {2}, but it does not contain their union {1, 2}.

A sigma-algebra must be closed under countable unions, which includes a union of two sets. Thus 𝒜 ∪ ℬ fails the requirement even though each collection separately satisfies it.

To obtain the smallest sigma-algebra containing both, one must add the missing sets; here that gives all subsets of Ω.

cards.title: A prime test that can be fooled
cards.front:
Fermat’s little theorem says that if p is prime and a is not divisible by p, then ap−1 ≡ 1 (mod p). A proposed test therefore declares an odd integer n prime whenever 2n−1 ≡ 1 (mod n).

Show that n = 341 fools this test. Show that 341 is composite and that it passes the stated test. You may use 341 = 11 × 31 and 2¹⁰ = 1024; explain the modular steps without expanding 2³⁴⁰.

Allow about 4 minutes to answer and 1 minute for feedback. Stop at 60 minutes total. Read the feedback once, then move on.
cards.back:
The factorization 341 = 11 × 31 shows that 341 is composite.

Since 1024 = 3 × 341 + 1, we have 2¹⁰ ≡ 1 (mod 341). Raising both sides to the 34th power gives 2³⁴⁰ ≡ 1 (mod 341).

So 341 passes the test despite being composite. Fermat’s theorem gives a necessary condition for primality in this setting; reversing the implication is invalid.

cards.title: A limit on comparison sorting
cards.front:
A deterministic algorithm sorts four distinct items using only comparisons of two items. Each comparison has two possible outcomes because all items are distinct.

Prove that some input order requires at least five comparisons. Count the possible input orders and compare that count with the most outcome sequences available from four comparisons. You do not need to construct a sorting algorithm.

Allow about 4 minutes to answer and 1 minute for feedback. Stop at 60 minutes total. Read the feedback once, then move on.
cards.back:
There are 4! = 24 possible orders of the four distinct items. A correct comparison-based algorithm must distinguish all of them.

If every input used at most four comparisons, its binary decision tree would have depth at most 4 and at most 2⁴ = 16 leaves. That is too few to distinguish 24 orders.

Therefore at least one input requires more than four comparisons, hence at least five. This is a worst-case lower bound; it does not say every input requires five.
